india-56a8e96e09.headline: How will the U.S.’s Sanctioning Act affect India? | Explained
india-56a8e96e09.source: India Latest News: Top National Headlines Today & Breaking News | The Hindu
india-56a8e96e09.fulltext:
The story so far:
U.S. President Donald Trump has signed into law the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act, 2026, which could see tariffs of up to 100% being levied on imports from India if it continues to import oil from Russia. This Act, therefore, has significant implications for India with regard to its export ambitions and energy security. The Indian government’s concerns over the tariffs have so far gone unheeded.
Why did the U.S. introduce this law?
The initial purpose of the Act — proposed by the late Senator Lindsey O. Graham and named after him — was to cut off financing for Russia so as to choke its funding of its war with Ukraine. To this end, the Act provides for sanctions to be levied on Russia’s top leadership and its biggest energy customers.
Recently, the ‘and Iran’ part of the title was added to the Act to convey that such measures are also aimed at Iran. The text was amended to say that sanctions on Iran would be levied for another five years until 2031.
What does the Act say about tariffs?
For India, the most crucial aspect of the Act is what it says about countries that import Russian oil. Thirty days after its enactment, the Act allows the U.S. to impose a 100% tariff on goods originating in a country that meets one of two broad criteria. The first is a country that was among the five largest importers, by total volume, of crude oil or natural gas from Russia during the 12 months preceding the Act’s enactment, and that continues to import oil or gas from Russia after the 30-day period.
This is the criterion that will likely impact India. China and India are the top two importers of Russian crude oil. Russian crude oil has accounted for a rising share of India’s oil imports since February 2026, when the U.S. Supreme Court struck down Mr. Trump’s tariff regime, including the 25% punitive tariff he had imposed on India for its Russian oil imports.
According to the latest data, Russia accounted for more than 51% of India's crude oil imports in July 2026. Scaling this back drastically within 30 days, at a time when passage through the Strait of Hormuz is still constrained, will likely be impossible for India.
The second criterion for imposition of tariffs is whether a country was among the top five nations “facilitating Russian oil sanctions evasion during the 12 months preceding the date of the enactment of the Act”. India runs a much lower risk of qualifying for tariffs under this criterion, as Indian oil marketing companies have repeatedly said that all their purchases have been made without violating sanctions.
Will these be the total tariffs on imports from India?
No. The law clearly states that an import tariff imposed under this Act “shall be in addition to any other duty” levied on any good. This includes tariffs imposed under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, which allows the United States Trade Representative to investigate and retaliate against foreign trade practices that harm American commerce, and Section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act of 1962, which authorises the U.S. President to restrict imports or impose tariffs if an investigation finds that foreign goods threaten national security.
These two other Acts are important because India is among the countries that already face tariffs under them. That is, the U.S. Trade Representative used Section 301 to investigate American trade partners to determine whether they had done enough to stop the import of goods made using forced labour. Based on its findings, it imposed a tariff of 10% on imports from India. In addition, Mr. Trump had widened existing tariffs under Section 232 to include steel, aluminium, copper, and related derivative products, and hiked the rate to 50%. Since this applied to all countries equally, it placed India on a level playing field with its competitors.
A potential 100% tariff on top of that will severely dent India’s competitiveness in these sectors.
Will these tariffs come into force immediately?
No. A period of 30 days has to elapse before the U.S. can determine whether countries are still importing oil and gas from Russia. It is only after this period that the U.S. can levy the tariffs under the law. Further, the text of the Act says that the U.S. Trade Representative, in consultation with the Secretary of State and the Secretary of Energy would, within 180 days after the initial imposition of tariffs, again review the countries that are the five largest importers of crude oil and natural gas from Russia based on the most recent 12-month period.
What is the potential impact on India’s economy?
The impact on India’s economy has to be looked at in terms of two eventualities. The first is if India continues to buy large quantities of Russian oil and bears the tariffs. The second is if India cuts back on Russian oil imports and manages to have the potential tariffs removed.
In the event that India continues to buy Russian oil and bears the tariffs, we can look at what happened during the period when the 50% tariffs were in force, between August 2025 and February 2026, to gauge the likely impact.
The April to August 2025 period saw merchandise exports to the U.S. grow nearly 18% compared with the same period the previous year. While some of this was due to front-loaded exports in anticipation of future tariffs, it nevertheless highlighted the strong momentum of exports from India to the U.S. However, over the longer April 2025 to February 2026 period, exports to the U.S. grew at a much slower 3.8%, showing a substantial slowdown in exports after August, when the tariffs came into effect.
Conversations with exporters at the time showed that many of them were sharing the cost of the higher tariffs with their U.S. customers in order to retain them. At the rate of 50%, this was already a body blow to most of them. These exporters will not be in a position to share a 100% tariff.
Historical data, however, show that India has chosen to comply with U.S. pressure to reduce oil imports from countries such as Venezuela, Iran, and Russia. If India again cuts down on Russian oil imports, this could have serious ramifications for the supply and price of fuel within India. At a time when the Strait of Hormuz is constrained, and oil prices are again comfortably above $100 a barrel, India will likely find it very expensive to look for newer sources of oil. For Indian citizens, this could translate into more fuel price hikes. For the government, such hikes would be politically unpalatable since there are several key State elections next year.
Is there a third way out?
The Act includes a provision for a waiver of tariffs. The U.S. President can waive the tariffs once he has submitted to Congress a certification in writing that the waiver “is in the national interests of the U.S.” and a report explaining the basis for the certification.
The other way out is if Russia signs “a peace agreement that is accepted by the free and independent Government of Ukraine” and ceases “all military hostilities against and any activities to overthrow, dismantle, and subvert the Government of Ukraine”.

global-economics-6bb0b3e6e9.headline: From 18% to 100%: How the new US law changes the tariff risk for India
global-economics-6bb0b3e6e9.fulltext:
The significance for India lies in the gap between the 18% tariff rate referred to in an earlier February 6 joint statement and the new law’s provision allowing tariffs of up to 100%. GTRI said the legislation puts India and China at direct risk because the US can target imports from the five largest foreign buyers of Russian crude oil and natural gas.
What has changed?
The earlier 18% figure represented a tariff rate mentioned in the February 6 joint statement, according to the GTRI report. The new legislation, however, creates a statutory route for much higher tariffs, with the maximum potentially reaching 100%.
GTRI said Washington could potentially use this tariff threat to pressure India to sharply reduce purchases of Russian oil and make concessions under a bilateral trade agreement.
However, the 100% rate is a maximum possibility under the law, not a tariff that has already been imposed on Indian goods. The actual impact will depend on the rates, products and implementation schedule announced by the US administration.
When will India know the actual tariff?
The law is set to take effect within 30 days. During this period, the US Trade Representative will identify countries that could be targeted and recommend tariff rates, according to GTRI.
The report said the countries concerned would normally have 180 days to reduce Russian energy purchases or negotiate with Washington. It also noted that the US President could shorten this period.
This means Indian exporters currently face uncertainty rather than a confirmed 100% tariff across their shipments.
Why Russian oil matters
GTRI said discounted Russian crude has helped reduce India’s import bill, strengthen energy security and contain inflation. It therefore cautioned against exchanging long-term energy interests for temporary tariff relief.
The think tank said even reducing Russian oil purchases or signing a trade agreement may not prevent future US action under Section 301, sectoral tariffs or other trade laws.
For now, GTRI said India should continue buying Russian oil while it remains commercially competitive and negotiate firmly with Washington. The impact on Indian exports can be assessed more accurately only after the US announces the tariff rate, products covered and implementation schedule.

Semicon India 2026: India’s chip bet shifts to startup capital
                    India’s semiconductor strategy is shifting towards chip design and startup funding, but founders say customer adoption, fabrication access and commercial scale remain critical hurdles.
                                    
            
        At Semicon India 2026, the government’s semiconductor strategy moved beyond building fabs and packaging plants towards a more direct bet on Indian chip startups, including a plan to co-invest alongside private venture capital.
Several announcements highlighted the government’s push to build a semiconductor ecosystem beyond fabs. Applied Materials announced a $5 billion investment over the next decade under its India Vision 2035, including deeper R&D, supply-chain expansion and a proposed 140-acre advanced semiconductor research park.
Tata Electronics signed seven MoUs, including with Nexperia on wafer manufacturing, assembly and testing, and with Ascendas First Space for a 363-acre vendor park in Dholera. According to the Press Bureau of Information (PIB), the government also announced six ChipIN regional centres, while Suchi Semicon and eInfochips exchanged their first batch of commercial devices, signalling a move towards production and commercialisation.
Lam Research announced plans to invest around ₹10,000 crore in India over the coming years, including a proposed silicon-component manufacturing facility and expansion of its R&D operations.
Additionally, under Semicon 2.0 announced in July, the government said it will match private capital raised by eligible semiconductor design startups and take an equity stake on the same terms as private investors, with plans to exit as companies mature. The ₹1.275 lakh crore programme also expands support across design, equipment and materials, fabs, advanced packaging, R&D and talent.
The shift comes as private capital into India’s semiconductor ecosystem grows, although funding remains concentrated in a relatively small number of companies and cities.
Tracxn’s September 2026 report put cumulative semiconductor funding in India at $1.4 billion, with $776 million raised in the last two years. The report recorded $228 million across 30 funding rounds in 2026 year-to-date.
Yet the more important question is whether this capital can produce companies that move beyond chip design and become scaled semiconductor businesses.
From subsidy to co-investment
The government’s new model addresses a problem in semiconductor investing, which is long development cycles and high upfront costs.
Sagar Vishnoi, director and co-founder of Future Shift Labs, said the model addresses a “genuine structural gap in India’s semiconductor ecosystem.” He said semiconductor investing has a different risk profile from conventional technology because development cycles are longer, upfront costs are higher, and returns take longer to materialise.
“We are beginning to see that change, with around 20 chip-design startups attracting roughly ₹800 crore in venture funding. But that is still relatively modest for a sector of this scale and ambition,” Vishnoi said. “The significance of the government’s VC-matching model is that public capital can help absorb some of that early-stage risk and give private investors greater confidence to participate.”
However, he cautioned that the government should remain a “catalytic co-investor rather than become a substitute for private capital.”
Vishnu Das, advisor at the Foundation for Science Innovation & Development, IISc, and former principal investor at Celesta Capital, said the matching mechanism can reduce some of the risk involved in getting from design to first silicon and production.
“But funding is really only one part of the equation,” Das told ETEntrepreneur. “You can build a technically very good chip and still struggle to get customers to qualify it and switch from established suppliers.” He said startups need to work closely with anchor customers, design around their requirements, and demonstrate reliability at scale so early pilots become repeat orders.
According to the PIB, 20 of the 105 semiconductor startups supported during the first phase have already secured VC funding, and Semicon 2.0 aims to expand the design ecosystem to 200 startups.
Ashwini Vaishnaw, the Union Minister for Electronics and Information Technology, said at Semicon India 2026 that ₹1 lakh crore has been committed to the Semicon 2.0 ecosystem. This investment is expected to generate significant economic activity and nearly 1 lakh new jobs in the semiconductor sector. Companies will announce their investments over the next two to three years after securing board and shareholder approvals.
The customer is shaping the chip
That transition is also changing the traditional relationship between chipmakers and customers.
Aravind Prasad, founder and CEO of Deepgrid Semi, described it as a reversal of the conventional model.
“For 30 years, chipmakers built general-purpose silicon, and customers just built around it. AI has inverted that,” Prasad told ETEntrepreneur. “Now it says, ‘You design according to our requirements, not the way you used to, and then we work the other way around.’”
Deepgrid is developing transformer-native SoCs for ADAS, robotics and autonomous systems. Its technology has been deployed on FPGAs in humanoids, autonomous mobile robots and automated guided vehicles, and the company is seeking ₹25 crore for tape-out. It expects that to bring chipset costs down from around ₹35,000 to ₹3,000, potentially enabling mass-market deployment.
The company’s first chip, Prasad said, was designed around requirements from the ADAS and defence sectors, rather than as a general-purpose processor. “We will be co-designing with customers, as customer proximity is critical, and nobody is closer to Indian customers than Indian chip companies,” he said.
Ganesh Dabbikar, founder and director of KriSemi Design Technologies, similarly said “domain-specific workloads now dictate silicon design.” He said hyper-specialised AI and edge-computing applications are creating demand for custom architectures, allowing Indian startups to co-design specialised IP with niche global customers.
KriSemi, founded in 2018, provides chip-design, embedded systems, SATCOM and board-design services to semiconductor and defence customers, with more than 100 professionals and projects spanning ASIC, FPGA, RF/mixed-signal and photonic ICs.
For Lightspeed Photonics, the customer-led shift is playing out at the infrastructure layer. The company is developing compact optical interconnects for AI data centres, with its LightKonnect product designed to sit next to processors on a PCB rather than requiring a major chip-package redesign. It has raised $8.5 million to date, including $6.5 million in a pre-series A funding round led by pi Ventures, and is working towards commercial production and a photonics packaging pilot line in India.
Its CEO Rohin Y said specialised AI, edge and data-centre workloads are increasingly influencing future chip architectures.
“A diverse set of applications, led by data centres, edge and AI inference, are becoming major drivers of future chip architectures,” Rohin said. “For Indian startups, this means identifying niche areas and white spaces where we can build scalable chips beyond standard products used in traditional industries.”
Design is scaling, manufacturing remains the next test
The debate, however, is no longer simply about whether India needs fabs.
Das said funding can reduce some of the risk between design and first silicon, but customer qualification remains a major hurdle.
“The next step is working closely with anchor customers, designing around their requirements, and demonstrating reliability at scale so early pilots become repeat orders,” he said. “We’re already seeing Indian startups enter customer trials; the real test now is whether they can turn those trials into design wins and sustained commercial volumes.”
Vishnoi similarly points to the gap between IP creation and commercial deployment.
“Startups need affordable access to fabrication and tape-outs, testing and packaging infrastructure, product validation and qualification, and, importantly, support to move from small prototype runs to commercial volumes,” Vishnoi said. “The real measure of success will not simply be how many chips India designs, but how many of those designs ultimately make it into products that are manufactured, adopted, and sold at scale.”
Rohin takes a more infrastructure-heavy view. He argued that next-generation semiconductor innovation will increasingly depend on fabrication and materials capabilities.
“It is practically impossible to innovate only at the design level,” Rohin said. “We cannot depend indefinitely on foreign tape-outs for local consumption, nor can we move beyond standard chip design and production capabilities without thinking about the future of fabs themselves.” He said India should encourage startups to build small in-house fabs and pilot lines, supported by capital.
Deepgrid’s Prasad, however, sees fabrication differently.
“Fabrication is not the challenge for Indian chip startups today,” he said. “NVIDIA doesn't own a fab; AMD doesn't own a fab. We follow the same model: we design, we own the IP, and world-class foundries manufacture for us.”
He said the challenge emerges later, when startups need guaranteed capacity for volume production. “When we need guaranteed supply, that’s when domestic fabs in India will come on board,” Prasad said.
From chip startups to companies of scale
The final challenge is therefore not just producing more Indian chip designs, but building companies that can capture value beyond engineering services or individual IP licences.
Dabbikar identifies four requirements for global scale, namely patient capital, domestic testing and advanced packaging, access to tier-one OEMs and stronger global IP protection.
“Scaling globally requires moving beyond design talent to building robust semiconductor commercialization ecosystems,” he said. Dabbikar believes that key elements include securing long-term venture capital to navigate extended silicon cycles, establishing a robust domestic infrastructure for advanced packaging, connecting directly with tier-1 OEMs for market integration, and implementing clear patent strategies to protect innovations.
Das argued that Indian startups should focus on markets such as industrial chips, edge AI, automotive electronics and power semiconductors, using the domestic market to build early customers before expanding globally.
“Indian startups don’t necessarily need to go head-to-head with NVIDIA or Qualcomm to build global businesses,” he said. “There are opportunities in areas like industrial chips, edge AI, automotive electronics, and power semiconductors where they can use India’s domestic market to win early customers and build a track record.”
The key, he added, is to “think like product companies rather than engineering companies” by building differentiated products that can be sold repeatedly across customers.
“Three things, in order: sockets, systems, and patience,” Prasad stressed.
“A chip business isn't built on tape-outs; it's built on qualifications,” he said. “When your chip gets designed into a meter, a truck, or a defense platform, it is going to stay there for the next 10 to 15 years.”
He argued that the next step is anchor purchase orders for Indian silicon. “Once a socket is confirmed, it is worth more than any grant,” Prasad said, adding that startups also need to build reference designs and complete systems around their chips.

Trump says US will form 'AI Force' and appoint an artificial intelligence tsar
- Published
US President Donald Trump has announced that he will form an "AI Force" and appoint an artificial intelligence tsar amid warnings about the emergent technology.
In a social media post on Saturday, he said his administration "will not in any way hinder or stifle the growth" of the industry, and pushed back against calls to slow down the development of AI until better safeguards are put in place.
His post came as a slew of warnings about the potential dangers of AI have spurred calls for coordinated action on the technology's development.
Trump offered no details or a timeline for his plan.
- Why Trump is all-in on AI despite the warnings 
  - Published3 days ago
"AI is the next Industrial Revolution, or Internet, but will be even larger and more impactful, possibly as much as 25% of our Country's GDP," he said on social media, adding that he wants the US to continue leading China in AI.
AI now sits at the heart of the US-China rivalry as the world's two largest economies seek to gain an edge in advanced tech, and it is expected to be discussed when Trump meets President Xi Jinping next week.
Meanwhile, Trump said his administration would use the existing criminal and civil justice system to target any bad actors using the AI.
He also repeated comments that criticism and concerns around the potential dangers of AI are a "hoax".
Claims by current and former researchers that the tech will endanger humanity - with one suggesting there is a greater than 10% chance of it "killing all humans" - have raised alarm bells in recent weeks.
Major AI companies have been racing to develop better systems, including creating what they call super intelligence - theoretical tech which is smarter than humans.
AI titans Anthropic, OpenAI and Google - the tech companies behind Claude, ChatGPT and Gemini, respectively - have also disclosed instances of security breaches or incidents in which their chatbots were used for "malicious activity".
Anthropic head Dario Amodei recently called for AI development to slow down and proposed industry-wide deceleration and regulation, as well as independent monitoring of AI model development.
Sam Altman of OpenAI and Elon Musk of xAI have both said they agree with his recommendations.
Jack Clark, co-founder of Anthropic, told BBC that a "kill switch" that can be checked by a third party may need to be mandatory for the industry.
The warnings have prompted US lawmakers to propose legislation around the technology but Altman suggested this week that Washington has struggled to keep pace with the new tech and how to regulate it. He said people should have more faith in AI firms to keep it safe.
"The world should trust that we are going to do the right thing because it's the right thing and we feel the magnitude of this," Altman told a conference in San Francisco.
In the UK, MPs across parties and peers have identified human rights risks posed by artificial intelligence and have argued that existing laws are ill-equipped to address the technology's rapid growth.
The Joint Committee on Human Rights (JCHR) has published a report calling for a new bill on AI to "address the scale and seriousness" of such threats.

A social media platform linked to China Central Television (CCTV) has accused American artificial intelligence (AI) developer Anthropic of creating severe data security risks, alleging that the company’s internal privacy frameworks permit user records to be shared with US intelligence agencies without formal legal oversight. The allegations, published on Saturday (September 19) by Yuyuantantian, an account affiliated with the Chinese state broadcaster, say that successive updates to Anthropic’s legal terms have systematically widened surveillance vulnerabilities for international users.
The criticism comes at a diplomatically sensitive moment, coming just as Beijing and Washington prepare to convene bilateral trade negotiations ahead of a planned meeting between Chinese President Xi Jinping and US President 
Donald Trump
 on September 24.
‘Anthropic makes 13 privacy tweaks’
According to the Yuyuantantian post (via Bloomberg), Anthropic has amended its official privacy documentation 13 separate times since 2023. The report highlighted specific adjustments governing how overseas consumer records are handled. As per the allegations, updated provisions enable user data originating in the 
European Union
, Canada, Brazil and South Korea to be transmitted straight to US servers.
The platform allegedly expanded its active data sources from three to six between June 2024 and September 2025. 
The post also claimed that Anthropic quietly revised its system terms in September of last year to automatically ingest user interactions for AI model training by default.
The publication pointed directly to disclosures inside Anthropic’s own reporting, noting that the startup admitted to handing technical threat indicators over to US intelligence agencies after accusing certain Chinese enterprises of carrying out unauthorised model-distillation operations.
Yuyuantantian further alleged that the AI firm is deliberately cultivating close ties with American defense and intelligence apparatuses through its recruitment pipeline.

SFAL signs seven MoUs to strengthen India’s semiconductor startup ecosystem
The partnerships span semiconductor research, design, manufacturing, electronic design automation (EDA), workforce development, investment, technology commercialisation and startup acceleration.
SFAL has partnered with IISc Centre for Nano Science and Engineering (CeNSE), FourFront Ltd., PeachTree Elevate, Aarayaa Advisory Services, Kaynes Semicon, WOWSEMI Foundation and Silvaco Inc.
The partnerships are aimed at connecting startups with academia, manufacturers, technology providers, investors, and industry stakeholders, providing access to expertise, technology, talent, capital, and market opportunities.
From research to manufacturing
The collaboration with Kaynes Semicon will provide startups exposure to semiconductor manufacturing requirements and support the journey from technology development and validation to production and commercialisation.
FourFront's partnership will focus on India's indigenous automotive electronics and semiconductor ecosystem, including advanced power electronics, EV architectures and active EMI suppression systems.
Silvaco will provide access to semiconductor design and EDA tools, technical knowledge and industry perspectives to support technology development and validation.
Building talent and investment readiness
On the research and talent side, IISc CeNSE, WOWSEMI Foundation and PeachTree Elevate will support research collaboration, semiconductor skill development, startup mentoring and capability building.
The partnership with Aarayaa Advisory Services will focus on investment readiness for semiconductor startups, including fundraising, financial planning, investor engagement and business development.
Karnataka IT/BT and E-Governance Minister Priyank Kharge said the partnerships would help connect startups with research, technology, manufacturing, talent, investment and global markets as India builds deeper capabilities across the semiconductor value chain.
The seven MoUs are aligned with the broader objectives of the India Semiconductor Mission. They are intended to create a pathway for emerging companies from research and innovation through technology development, validation, manufacturing, commercialisation and market adoption.

deep-tech-2bd88722eb.headline: Fortaegis Technologies Raises $50 Million Series A to Deploy Hardware-Rooted Quantum-Safe Secure Compute Architecture
deep-tech-2bd88722eb.fulltext:
Amsterdam-based hardware security startup Fortaegis Technologies has closed an oversubscribed $50 million Series A funding round to accelerate commercial production and global deployment of its full-stack Secure Compute architecture. Led by returning investor Serendipity Capital, the syndicate includes strategic semiconductor, industrial, and defense backers TEL Venture Capital (the CVC arm of Tokyo Electron), ASML, TNO, Prodrive Technologies, NP-Hard Ventures, NovaCapital, Access Ventures, and Coalition Capital.
The company’s executive leadership and board include Ilyas Khan (Founder of Quantinuum) as Chairman, Boudewijn Wijnands as Founder and CEO, and Chris Miller (author of Chip War) as a U.S. Board Member. Fortaegis’s technology addresses hardware security threats posed by high-throughput AI workloads and post-quantum decryption risks. The Fortaegis Silicon Platform provides a full-stack architecture spanning hardware, firmware, cryptography, and software that roots security directly in physical silicon properties.
By extracting cryptographic entropy from microscopic physical manufacturing variations in silicon, the architecture generates dynamic, quantum-resistant encryption keys on demand without storing keys permanently on-chip, eliminating key-theft attack vectors. Fortaegis reports holding 17 patents (with 14 pending) and achieving secure machine-to-machine connection speeds over 200 times faster than conventional software cryptographic approaches in customer evaluations. Capital from the round will scale FPGA deployment and advance its custom ASIC development pipeline across data center, defense, telecommunications, and autonomous infrastructure markets.

Chip foundries better insulated in an AI slowdown than Asia-Pacific tech peers, S&P says
Contract chipmakers like TSMC are well protected against spending contractions by hyperscalers, based on stress tests by the ratings agency
As market fears mount over waning Big Tech spending and calls to slow down frontier artificial intelligence development, Asia-Pacific semiconductor foundries are better positioned to withstand a potential downturn in AI investment than other tech hardware firms in the region, according to S&P Global Ratings.
In a report published on Thursday, the rating agency said it had stress tested four key Asia-Pacific sectors – foundries, memory manufacturers, cooling component suppliers and original design manufacturers that assemble servers – against two downside scenarios for the AI boom.
The first possibility involved a drop in capital expenditure from major hyperscalers like Amazon and Microsoft. The second stemmed from bottlenecks that could delay AI projects, such as power grid constraints and land scarcity.

deep-tech-165f4bca80.headline: ‘Water could become a constraint on expansion of semiconductor industry’
deep-tech-165f4bca80.fulltext:
India’s semiconductor build-out must factor in water recycling, chemical management and other sustainability safeguards at the design stage itself, as trying to retrofit these systems after fabrication plants become operational could prove significantly more difficult and costly, experts said at a panel discussion on Saturday at Semicon India 2026.
Indumathy Nambi of IIT Madras, who moderated the session, said semiconductor manufacturing needs to be viewed through its entire lifecycle, from design to disposal. She highlighted the large quantities of water, energy, chemicals and materials used by fabs and called for the recovery and reuse of materials rather than treating waste only at the end of the manufacturing process.
With semiconductor manufacturing requiring large volumes of ultra-pure water, energy and chemicals, the experts said sustainability cannot be treated as an add-on once production begins.
“Right now we are in a hurry to probably start with the production and if we do not incorporate this during the design stage, it’s going to be even more technically and financially heavy to do those kind of retrofits,” said Prateek Bhatt, Business Director at Ecolab.
water circularity
Bhatt said water could become a major constraint on the expansion of India’s semiconductor industry. A single mega fab can consume around 10–15 million gallons of water a day, he said, warning that sourcing such volumes from groundwater would not be sustainable.
Bhatt argued that the industry needs to adopt water circularity by recycling and reusing water within facilities and minimising discharge into the environment.
According to Bhatt, global water circularity in semiconductor manufacturing is currently around 40–50 per cent, but the industry should aim for 80–95 per cent. He said technologies already exist to achieve higher levels of recycling, but they need to be incorporated into the design of individual facilities.
“The best way to do is to segregate the streams rather than blend them in the one place,” he said, explaining that separating wastewater streams makes it easier to treat and recycle them.
The need to plan for water management at the design stage is particularly important as semiconductor manufacturing processes become more advanced. Bhatt said that as chip node sizes decline, the number of rinses increases, meaning water consumption could rise further.
The panel also highlighted the challenges posed by chemicals used in semiconductor manufacturing, including per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS), often referred to as “forever chemicals”.
Vaidya Bharadwaj of Tokyo Electron said PFAS is used across semiconductor equipment and that while existing safety practices can address exposure within manufacturing facilities, the longer-term environmental challenge remains difficult.
“It’s an engineering problem that a single company or single country cannot solve. So it needs a lot of R&D. It needs time to solve,” he said, adding that collaboration across the industry would be required to develop alternatives.

Can Private Wealth Save India's Water And Wilderness?
- Economy
- Published on 19 Sept 2026 6:00 AM IST
In this edition of The Core Report, Shloka Nath: Founder and CEO, Dorahi, Mobilising Philanthropic Capital for India’s Climate Transition, Harish Yarlagadda: AIP Founder; Founder & Chief Mentor, Malaxmi Group; and Co-Founder, Dharmavana Nature Ark (DNA), Ravi Mariwala, Founder & Chairman Smaart Wateron why biodiversity, water reform and "unlock" capital, not more schemes, will decide India's climate future.
The Gist
- Shloka Nath emphasizes the interconnectedness of climate and development agendas.
- Harish Yarlagadda highlights the importance of biodiversity and moral responsibility in addressing ecological challenges.
- Dr. Ravi Mariwala focuses on water management and the need for effective sewage treatment to ensure public health and environmental sustainability.
NOTE: This transcript contains the host's monologue and includes interview transcripts by a machine. Human eyes have gone through the script but there might still be errors in some of the text, so please refer to the audio in case you need to clarify any part. If you want to get in touch regarding any feedback, you can drop us a message on feedback@thecore.in.
Hi, and welcome to this Core Reports special edition. We are talking today about how climate can be addressed through wealth, or more specifically, how Indian philanthropy can address one of the most defining and fundamental challenges we face: climate change. We will approach this in two or three different ways, but we are going to explore it through the eyes of people who have done work on the ground, through their experiences of how they have tried to address a particular problem and then scaled up. We will also try to understand where they want to take this world, and how they envision a world that is, let's say, a better place to live in.
To do all of that, I am joined by three guests: Shloka Nath, who has been mobilising a lot of philanthropic capital and previously served as CEO of the India Climate Collaborative; to my right, Harish Yarlagadda, founder and chief mentor of the Malakshmi Group and co-founder of the Dharmavana Nature Arc (DNA); and finally, Dr. Ravi Mariwala, founder and CEO of Smart Water, who is also a promoter at Marico Limited. Thank you all for joining me.
Let me start with you, Shloka, and get a broad sense of things. There is capital today, there is wealth in this country — we all understand that we want to do something about climate, and many indeed are doing something about it. So how would you define the scope of what we want to do, in the context of how we are thinking about it?
Shloka Nath, Founder and CEO, Dorahi, Mobilising Philanthropic Capital for India’s Climate Transition
That's a big question, but let me try to frame it with this one thought: there is no real division between a development agenda and a climate agenda, and I fear that is unfortunately where we are in terms of our mindset when we think about climate change. The development agenda *is* the climate agenda. Climate is the biggest force multiplier when it comes to our existing development constraints.
It is not a new problem that has suddenly been thrust upon us, and yet, in philanthropy, when we talk about capital, we talk about climate as something that arrived recently. In reality, it is entering through every single existing problem we already have. So how we choose to address that, we have to be very aware that today there is no critical pathway to sustainable development that is untouched by climate anymore. It doesn't exist.
So the first thing we have to do in philanthropy — and more broadly, when we think about the transition of India's economy — is accept that climate change *is* the development agenda. It underpins it, and we need to think more in terms of how we actually risk-proof that development agenda, and ensure that growth is not sacrificed because of this threat multiplier that is exacerbating our existing issues.
This has obviously been a live issue for a few years, and you have been at, perhaps, the epicentre of it, particularly from a philanthropy point of view. What would you say has been achieved in the last few years?
Shloka Nath
That's really interesting. When we first set up the ICC, we would go door to door and ask, "Do you know what climate change is?" I think the challenge today isn't that funders, bureaucrats, or implementers don't understand what climate change is.
We have a distinct problem compared to the Global North, where there is still a lot of climate denialism. Here, I think we're steeped in acceptance of the problem — the real challenge is that we don't seem to be able to create a whole that's greater than the sum of its parts.
We face coordination challenges and ecosystem challenges. For instance, most funders still want to "build the bridge," if I can use that analogy, but who is going to fund the engineers, the maps, the standards — everything it takes to ensure we don't end up with 20 bridges going to 20 different places? We have to be able to fund things in totality.
For example, say you want to fund a solar company. That means you also have to look at how women will be represented in the jobs that are created, how we think about regulation, and how we think about the standards for the technology involved. No one is funding those wider ecosystem pieces. So the challenge isn't really about whether we understand what climate is and whether we should address it — the challenge is whether we can build an entirely holistic approach to solving this problem, and ensure that the system has the agency to coordinate around it. I'm happy to talk more about this in detail, but that's what sits with me today.
Got it. Harish, you've been a power entrepreneur, working in the energy space more broadly, and then you transitioned — or additionally transitioned — into this work. Tell us about it.
Harish Yarlagadda, AIP Founder; Founder & Chief Mentor, Malaxmi Group; and Co-Founder, Dharmavana Nature Ark (DNA)
Fully transitioned, actually. So, building on what Shloka said — we really don't understand climate. I made money; I was a polluter, burning a lot of fossil fuel to make that money. At some point in life, you realise that what you're doing isn't the right thing to do.
Whenever we talk about climate, whenever we talk about the planet, we really only talk about ourselves. We don't talk about the other billion living organisms on this planet. We divide ourselves into countries and languages, not realising that we all descend, mitochondrially, from the same lineage. Human beings are very confused, and the cultures and religions we grew up with developed, in part, through falsehoods. The day we invented language, the first thing that came out was lies, and through those lies we became who we are today. We are heavily influenced by the things around us.
When that realisation hit me, I understood that I needed to widen my circle of moral concern. Today, my circle of moral concern extends to myself, my family, my region, my friends, my country at most, to human beings but not beyond that. That is where it really struck me, and I decided the first place to focus was biodiversity, because it isn't only about protecting species that share this planet with us in a symbiotic relationship, it's also about carbon capture, usage, and storage (CCUS). That's why, as a first step, I exited most of my power plants it took some time and now I concentrate mainly on biodiversity as a non-profit, alongside a few sustainability-focused companies working on water management, compressed biogas (CBG), and climate resilience.
And biodiversity specifically — did some other thought process lead you there? You seem to be among the few, if not the only person, I've encountered who has focused on biodiversity as a specific challenge.
Harish Yarlagadda
Yes. Before this interview, I was chatting with my fellow panellists about this. Biodiversity is genuinely difficult work. I could plant a Miyawaki forest, but that isn't biodiversity. Many people mistake "greening", say, greening Haridwar or greening the planet — for biodiversity. It isn't. What lives in the rhizosphere, where plant roots grow, accounts for 25% of living organisms. That's what we have to protect; everything else follows automatically. That's where most of the real action is happening.
Think of the movie *Avatar* — the way life on that planet connects through mycelium and mycorrhizal fungi. That's the kind of connection we need to build here. That's why I chose biodiversity as my first step.
And by definition, biodiversity is about scale, we'll spend some time on that later. Ravi, where did Smart Water begin, and what was the inspiration?
Ravi Mariwala: Founder & Chairman Smaart Water
The inspiration was very simple. I was building a house about 15 kilometres outside Mumbai, as the crow flies, and found there was no piped water. Even in places like Panvel or Khopoli, the same problem exists, and it's fairly uniform across the country: urban and peri-urban areas lack water, and in rural areas, people often have to fetch fresh water themselves.
I was staying at a friend's house, trying to finish construction, and he said, "Ravi, this is a problem out here." I said no, it's not, he had a great water system, except he had to press a button to switch on the generator that drove it. I asked why that was necessary, and realised there was nothing technologically new about his setup, so I decided to build my own.
Being a young engineer with a bit of hubris, tempered somewhat now, after seeing what's really happening in the water sector — I calculated that I would need exactly 481 watts to run a system for a five-bedroom house. I like numbers. So I went to the market, bought pumps, the most inefficient ones available, with an efficiency of just 27% (which, as it turns out, has much larger implications for the country) and it took me five and a half months to build the system.
Why so long? Because I needed a plumber, a mason, and an electrician together at the same time, and the odds of getting all three in one place were less than 1%. It took five and a half months, with many modifications, because the engineering wasn't perfect at first. I also learned that peri-urban areas lack trained plumbers and electricians; masons have practical experience but not formal training; and the materials commonly used aren't the right ones. Eventually it worked, and it still works today — the only thing I keep replacing is capacitors, because power quality in those areas remains poor.
A friend then asked, "You built this for yourself — why not build one for me?" Then another friend asked. I realised we were, in effect, in business the entrepreneurial instinct kicked in. I built six systems with my own hands (I enjoy building things myself) and sold them within three weeks.
At the time, I was running a lab that analysed water and food, and the data started "speaking" to me — I could look at water test results and conceptualise treatment systems almost intuitively. My engineering background helped a great deal with that analytical work. That's how it started, and I took it one piece at a time. Today, we provide the "last-mile" solution for gated communities and individual homes — just a month ago, we added a kitchen filtration product, something I had resisted for a while, and now we offer a complete, full-stack water solution.

India’s medical device sector has grown from a $5 billion industry in 2020–21 to $18 billion, reflecting the country’s expanding capabilities in medical technology manufacturing and its transition from import dependence towards greater self-sufficiency. The sector’s growth, supported by government policies and increased manufacturing activity, was a key focus of the opening day of the 32nd edition of Medical Fair India 2026, organised by Messe Düsseldorf India at the Bombay Exhibition Centre, Mumbai.
The three-day exhibition, being held from 17–19 September 2026, commenced with a lamp-lighting and ribbon-cutting ceremony, followed by a welcome address by Messe Düsseldorf India executives Mr Lars Wismer, Regional Head of Messe Düsseldorf for Asia (MDfA); Mr Ajay Kumar Gulati, General Manager, Messe Düsseldorf India; and Dr Rajiv Chhibber, Joint Forum Coordinator, Association of Indian Medical Device Industry (AiMeD) and Member, Advisory Committee, Medical Fair India 2026.
The opening session, the 11th International Healthcare Conference, featured Homer Chang, Director General, Taipei Economic and Cultural Center in Mumbai; Jamie Scattergood, Deputy Head of Mission, British Deputy High Commission, Mumbai; Dr Hui-Chen Su, Director, International Medical Center and Attending Neurologist, Department of Neurology, National Cheng Kung University Hospital; Sanjay Jha, Founder, Apaan Medtech; Khushbu Sharma, Joint Director, Voice of Healthcare; and Ajay Kumar Gulati, General Manager, Messe Düsseldorf India Pvt. Ltd.
Medical Fair India 2026 provided a platform for healthcare professionals, hospital procurement leaders, manufacturers, technology providers, distributors and other stakeholders to explore innovations and solutions shaping the healthcare ecosystem. Medical Fair India 2026 hosted insightful discussions on emerging topics, including future-ready hospitals, digital and sustainable healthcare systems, international partnerships in healthcare innovation, research and clinical excellence, and the integration of artificial intelligence in healthcare. Conversations also emphasised the need for pragmatic policies that support investment in manufacturing, particularly in terms of capital expenditure and operational expenditure, while addressing the needs of both smaller enterprises and larger manufacturers.
Speaking at the press conference, Dr Rajiv Chhibber, Joint Forum Coordinator, Association of Indian Medical Device Industry (AiMeD) and Member, Advisory Committee, Medical Fair India 2026, highlighted the sector’s growth and the policy support driving its development. He said, “The medical device sector has grown into a significant industry. In 2020–21, it was a $5 billion sector, and today it has grown to $18 billion. For a long time, medical devices were considered an import-dependent sector, but with the policies of the central and state governments, the industry is moving towards self-sufficiency. Manufacturing has increased by more than 100% in India, supported by initiatives such as the PLI and PRIP schemes. Today, our medical exports reach around 187 countries. The medical device sector, which was once seen as a smaller subsector of the pharmaceutical industry, has become an integral part of the healthcare sector.”
He also added, “We also need to focus on patient safety, ethical marketing practices and pricing, with the NPPA taking pricing-related matters seriously. Regulators must understand that medical devices are different from pharmacology. As technology advances, manufacturers need encouragement to invest in innovation, while ensuring that medical technology remains affordable in terms of both price and quality.”
Mr Lars Wismer, Regional Head of Messe Düsseldorf for Asia (MDfA), highlighted India’s growing significance in the global MedTech market and its expanding role as a manufacturer and supplier. He said, “India is definitely a growing market of the future, and we at Messe Düsseldorf for Asia are particularly focused on the country in the MedTech sector. India has come a long way from being a major importer to a market where more and more production is taking place. It is becoming a MedTech powerhouse, not only for the region but also for the world. Compared to Europe, the adoption rate in Asia is much higher, making Asian economies, especially India, an important market. India plays a significant role, not just as a customer but also as a manufacturer and supplier.” He added, “Medical Fair India provides a platform for knowledge exchange. It is not just about bringing new products and innovations together with buyers, but also about exchanging ideas, experiencing innovation and creating conversations around these developments.”
Focusing on established companies, small and medium enterprises, innovators and startups, Mr Ajay Kumar Gulati, General Manager, Messe Düsseldorf India, said, “We strive to bring small and medium enterprises, innovators and startups onto the same platform as large corporates, giving them an opportunity to meet and connect with the wider healthcare industry. This includes a broad range of technologies, from surgical devices and cardiac implants to imaging and other health technology solutions. The Mumbai edition is not only about bringing innovations and new products together with buyers, but also about exchanging ideas and experiencing innovation. Maharashtra is a hub for medical manufacturing, with several players operating out of the state. We are also seeing significant growth in AI within the MedTech industry, and the intention is to ensure that its implementation helps make healthcare more affordable and supports the growth of the sector.”
The government’s vision of affordability, availability and accessibility has evolved, with Medical Fair India 2026, supported by AiMeD and other partners, adding a fourth ‘A’ – Advancements. This reflects the growing emphasis on innovation and ensuring access to the latest and most advanced healthcare technologies.
Medical Fair India 2026 features international participation from Brazil, China, Germany, India, Italy, Japan, Malaysia, Singapore, South Korea and the United States of America. The initiative reflects the growing importance of strengthening India’s medical device manufacturing ecosystem and supply chain, while creating opportunities for manufacturers, technology providers, innovators and healthcare stakeholders to connect and explore business opportunities.
Messe Düsseldorf India extends its gratitude to all participants, exhibitors, and attendees for the success of the event and welcomes all to the next edition of Medical Fair India 2027 in New Delhi.

agritech-e6b13f2ec5.headline: Global ocean breaks records with 100 days of heat as El Niño adds new threat
agritech-e6b13f2ec5.fulltext:
- Data indicates that the global ocean sustained 100 consecutive days of record heat between June 2 and Sept. 10, and the high sea surface temperatures don’t give any indications of dropping in the near future.
- Experts attribute this episode to climate change, which they say the current El Niño weather pattern is amplifying.
- The record-breaking ocean heat has drawn concerns from experts about the effects on marine ecosystems, global weather patterns, and economies that depend on the ocean.
For 100 consecutive days between June 2 and Sept. 10, the global ocean outside of polar regions sustained record high average sea surface temperatures, according to data from the Climate Reanalyzer, a platform overseen by the University of Maine’s Climate Change Institute in the U.S.
On each of the 100 days, sea surface temperatures exceeded those on the same date in every other year on record since 1982. One of the highest readings occurred on Aug. 22, when global ocean sea surface temperatures reached 21.10° Celsius (69.98° Fahrenheit), according to the European Union’s Copernicus Climate Change Service. The Climate Reanalyzer reported temperatures climbing even higher between Aug. 22 and 27, with average ocean sea surface temperatures hitting 21.18° C (70.12° F). The platform draws on global sea surface temperature data recorded by the U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA).
These record temperatures are likely to remain elevated in the near future “given the state of the intensifying El Niño,” said Zachary Labe, a climate scientist at the U.S.-based nonprofit Climate Central, which communicates climate change science.
In a Sept. 10 press briefing that discussed the Climate Reanalyzer data, Labe said this record ocean heat is part of a long-term trend driven by the human-induced climate crisis. Without a reduction in greenhouse gases, he said the oceans will continue to warm.
“The driver of this record warmth is climate change,” he said, “and more than 90% of that excess heat from burning fossil fuels and those greenhouse gas emissions goes into the ocean.”
Experts say the unprecedented ocean heat is affecting marine ecosystems, global weather patterns, and economies that depend on the ocean for food security, livelihoods and coastal protection.
Ocean heat affects ecosystems, economies and health
The ocean absorbs an exceedingly high amount of heat each year. An analysis published in Advances in Atmospheric Science found that during 2025, the ocean absorbed 23 zettajoules, a quantity of energy equivalent to about 12 atomic bombs exploding in the ocean every second of every day. This was more than a 43% increase from the 16 zettajoules of heat the ocean took in during 2024.
Warming isn’t only affecting the sea surface layer, which extends to a depth of 200 meters (660 feet), but is reaching the deeper layers of the ocean, Labe said.
“All of this has significant impacts,” he said. “It impacts marine ecosystems. It shifts the geographies of all parts of the marine ecosystem food chain. It also impacts our economy — things like fisheries, tourism. It also impacts the physical climate system and weather. It can affect hurricanes, or it can affect marine ecosystems through coral.”
High sea temperatures are also known to drive land-based heatwaves, particularly in coastal areas, according to Claire Bergin, a researcher at the ICARUS Climate Research Centre at Ireland’s Maynooth University. Bergin collaborates with World Weather Attribution, a team of scientists who evaluate whether extreme weather events are attributable to climate change.
“There’s a direct link between increased sea temperatures and the intensity of land-based heat waves,” Bergin said in the press briefing. She said the heat waves Europe experienced over the summer, especially in coastal areas, were “exacerbated” by high sea surface temperatures.
Bergin said high sea temperatures were also linked to an increased wet bulb temperature on land — that is, the lowest temperature air that can be reached through evaporation, which has implications for humans’ ability to cool themselves. The higher the humidity, the more slowly moisture evaporates.
“Higher wet bulb temperatures negatively affect human health, as the high moisture content reduces our ability to regulate body temperature,” Bergin said. “It really shows that high sea temperatures are not confined to the sea; they affect marine life, the food and tourism industry, as well as humans’ day-to-day life.”
El Niño amplifies threats
While experts agree that climate change is primarily responsible for these high ocean sea surface temperatures, the current El Niño that began in June, which NOAA predicts to be “very strong,” could add fuel to the fire by amplifying the warming caused by human activity.
El Niño is a naturally occurring phenomenon that forms part of the El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO) cycle, a process in which sea surface temperatures and atmospheric pressure fluctuate across the tropical Pacific Ocean. The El Niño is the “warm” part of the cycle, occurring when Pacific trade winds weaken and warm water accumulates along the west coast of South America, which raises global temperatures.
Scientists expect the current El Niño will peak toward the end of 2026 and its force will continue into 2027.
However, the underlying trend of warming sea temperatures in response to climate change remains the primary concern for experts.
In the press briefing, Pickerell, the global director of the ocean program at the U.S.-based nonprofit World Resources Institute, emphasized the importance of reducing greenhouse gas emissions to keep that trend in check. This, he said, is not the responsibility of the individual, but of industry’s “big emitters” to transition away from oil and gas. Pickerell is also head of the secretariat at the High-Level Panel for a Sustainable Ocean Economy, a group of global leaders committed to the protection and sustainable management of the ocean.
The Paris Agreement, signed in 2015, intended to limit global warming to 1.5° C above preindustrial levels, a threshold scientists identified as being critical for avoiding the most dangerous impacts of climate change. But according to a new report from the U.N. Environment Programme, global temperatures are now likely to surpass that threshold within the next few years, pushing the planet into increasingly dangerous territory.
“Ultimately, we need to cut emissions,” Pickerell said. “That is the key thing here.”

agritech-c694cebac1.headline: Ecologists urge scientists and policymakers to study imminent ‘Super’ El Niño to prepare for the future
agritech-c694cebac1.fulltext:
As many as 188 of India’s scientists and ecologists jointly published an appeal to fellow researchers and field practitioners to prepare for the effects of upcoming El Niño — a global weather phenomenon that dampens the monsoon and leads to extreme hot and dry conditions in the subcontinent.
In the Pacific Ocean where El Niño originates, temperatures have steadily risen above the 0.5°C threshold, reaching +2.6°C in August 2026. Projections report possible anomalies of up to +4°C, which is higher than at any time in the past 1,000 years, based on reconstructions from coral cores, they said.
Over the upcoming months, the signatories warned, India’s natural systems are likely to experience a range of potentially devastating impacts as a result of El Niño. “These include widespread bleaching and mortality of coral, an increase in wildfires, and the death of large rainforest trees. With a high probability of drought and extreme heat conditions, this year’s El Niño is likely to be catastrophic for India’s farmers, fishers and shepherds as well. In addition, though, more subtle impacts on India’s nature — including delayed fruit production or changes in animal behaviour — could be equally important, but may be much less visible unless you are specifically looking for them,” they said.
The ‘Call to Action’ urges scientists to take advantage of the warning signs and mobilise as a community to document and study the impact of this event on India’s nature, arguing that better science and documentation are essential to preparing India for a climate resilient future.
Jayashree Ratnam, Scientist, National Centre for Biological Sciences, said in a release: “The coming year will be a litmus test for tropical forests and trees in India. Huge forest trees may appear indestructible, but in the Western Ghats, many of them are already near the limit of the heat they can tolerate. Large trees are especially susceptible to extended droughts. Trees in cities are also vulnerable because of the urban ‘heat island’ effect. It is vital to understand how the coming El Niño will impact trees and other plants — as these are the foundations on which all other life depends.”
“I have witnessed the devastating impacts of El Niños on India’s coral reefs before, and it is heartbreaking. Coral reefs can be remarkably resilient, but they need at least a decade after every major die-back of coral to show significant recovery. The last major El Niño was in 2024, and barely two years after that event, the projected scale and intensity of the heat wave that is currently headed our way is truly scary,” said Rohan Arthur, Marine Biologist with Nature Conservation Foundation.
Roxy Mathew Koll, Climate Scientist with the Indian Institute of Tropical Meteorology, also said India’s monsoon season is closing with a rainfall deficit, but the impacts may not end there. “They can creep into the seasons ahead and cascade through depleted soil moisture and water storage, land and marine heatwaves, stressed crops and livelihoods, forest fires, coral bleaching and less visible ecological changes. This gives us a short but valuable window to act. We must document these changes as they unfold, but also safeguard the ecosystems that remain and reduce the pressures already weakening them. What we learn and protect during this El Niño can help India prepare for a warmer and more volatile future.”
What is the 2026-27 ‘Super’ El Nino?
El Niño is a periodic climatic event (every 2-7 years) that is triggered by changed ocean circulation and warming in the eastern Pacific Ocean. Its consequences vary in different parts of the world. In India, El Niño events are typically associated with higher temperatures and a delayed/reduced monsoon. Within the Indian Ocean, the El Niño interacts with another system, the Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD), which can either dampen or amplify El Niño conditions regionally, according to the signatories.
“Although the last El Niño was only two years ago (2024), all signs are that we will see another event this year, but much larger in magnitude. Since May 2026, sea surface temperatures in the Pacific have exceeded 0.5°C above normal (the threshold for declaring an El Niño event), and those temperatures have been rising steadily, reaching +2.6°C in August 2026. Projections report possible anomalies of up to +4°C, which is higher than at any time in the past 1,000 years, based on reconstructions from coral cores,” the document explained.
It added that the main effects of the El Niño are expected to be felt in the northern hemisphere (including India) from November 2026 onwards into the next year. Indian Meteorological Department bulletins project El Niño effects until at least March 2027 (when their projections end), and the effects are likely to continue well beyond then.
“Based on earlier (albeit less extreme) El Niño events, the Indian landmass is expected to experience substantially hot and dry conditions, and weak monsoons. The surrounding seas are likely to witness marine heatwaves. Of course, the intensities are likely to vary across the geography of the country, and it is difficult to predict the magnitude of impact across India’s ecosystems. Much will depend on how the IOD develops over the coming months,” it said

LPU Students Turn Campus Innovation into a Defence-Tech Startup, Build Indigenous Drone Systems
Bureau,Odishabarta
New Delhi, [September 18, 2026]: Taking innovation beyond the classroom, students and alumni of ) have turned their expertise in drones, robotics and aeromodelling into a defence-focused deep-tech startup, ASTRA Drones & Robotics Solutions Pvt. Ltd. Founded by Siddharth Kushwaha, Anirban Sarkar and Sarthak Gaira, the startup is developing indigenous unmanned aerial systems for defence, surveillance, disaster response and industrial applications.
The founders’ journey began at LPU, where they were actively involved in the Renovation Tech Robotics and Aeromodelling (RTRA) Club, leading drone and robotics activities, mentoring students, conducting technical workshops and participating in national competitions. Their team earned recognition at several drone and robotics competitions hosted by leading IITs and NITs, building strong hands-on expertise in UAV development. The experience reflects the focus of LPU’s EduRevolution initiative, which encourages experiential learning, student-led innovation and practical application of classroom knowledge. LPU has also recognised Sarthak Gaira and Anirban Sarkar among its students involved in developing drone, VTOL, robotics and automation technologies for defence applications.
Their technical experience further expanded through work with the Indian Army’s Corps of Electronics and Mechanical Engineers (EME). During this period, the team contributed to the development and testing of multiple drone platforms, including surveillance drones, kamikaze drones and other specialised UAV systems. Such hands-on exposure is also aligned with LPU’s broader emphasis on research, innovation and industry-oriented learning.
Founded in January 2026, ASTRA today has a portfolio comprising FPV drones, surveillance drones, VTOL drones, training UAVs and customised drone platforms. In April 2026, the startup was selected for incubation at the Technology Business Incubator Foundation (TBIF), IIT Ropar, giving the young founders access to mentoring, research support and innovation infrastructure. The journey comes as LPU marks 25 Years of its institutional journey, with student entrepreneurship and innovation forming an increasingly visible part of its higher education ecosystem.
The company’s flagship innovation is its Counter-UAS Interceptor Drone System, a high-speed indigenous platform designed to detect, pursue and intercept hostile unmanned aerial systems. Developed with a focus on indigenous engineering and modularity, the platform aims to strengthen India’s counter-drone capabilities and support the country’s growing focus on self-reliance in defence technology.
Commenting on the development, Dr. Ashok Kumar Mittal, Founder Chancellor, Lovely Professional University, said, “Nothing is more fulfilling than seeing our students apply their knowledge for the nation. The journey of ASTRA is a strong example of how education, innovation and real-world exposure can empower young minds to create solutions with national impact. We are proud to see our students take their ideas beyond the classroom and contribute to India’s growing defence and deep-tech ecosystem.”
With its focus on indigenous engineering and next-generation UAV technologies, ASTRA aims to develop solutions for defence forces, government agencies, homeland security, disaster response, industrial applications and research, contributing to the vision of Atmanirbhar Bharat.

india-deep-tech-b16a1f2a26.headline: Bengaluru-based deeptech startup DheyaTech raises Rs 43 crore to scale gas turbine engine production
india-deep-tech-b16a1f2a26.fulltext:
Bengaluru-based deeptech startup DheyaTech has raised Rs 43 crore in a funding round led by Avaana Capital, with participation from existing investor Unimech Aerospace and Manufacturing.
The startup said it will use the fresh capital to scale production, establish a fully integrated testing facility for its gas turbine engines and work with domestic and global customers to accelerate deployment.
Founded in 2018 by Gurushankara K C, Abhinav Alva and Chetan Kumar, DheyaTech develops small gas turbine engines and energy systems for aerospace and power generation applications.
It develops small gas turbine engines and energy systems for aerospace and power generation applications.
Scaling gas turbine engine development
DheyaTech's engine portfolio spans thrust levels from 20 kgf to 400 kgf, targeting applications across advanced aerial mobility and energy systems.
Its gas turbines are moving towards commercial deployment, with flight trials targeted for the fourth quarter of 2026. The startup has also received confirmed orders from Indian and global original equipment manufacturers.
DheyaTech follows a platform-based approach designed to create a scalable family of engines across multiple thrust requirements and applications. Its in-house engineering team handles the development process from design to building and testing.
It has also developed an adaptive Engine Control Unit, or ECU, for its engine systems.
DheyaTech is pursuing airworthiness certification for its gas turbine engines through the Centre for Military Airworthiness and Certification, or CEMILAC, part of the Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO). CEMILAC is responsible for the airworthiness certification of military aircraft, engines and other airborne systems in India.
Gurushankara K C, CEO and co-founder of DheyaTech, said the funding will support the company's move towards production readiness.
“We have spent the last decade building deep expertise in gas turbine technology with the vision of creating world-class propulsion and energy solutions from India. This funding marks an important step in our journey from technology development to production readiness. We are focused on building a scalable family of engines, strengthening our testing capabilities and working closely with customers to take our technology into real-world applications. Our long-term goal is to make India more self-reliant in critical propulsion and energy technologies,” he said.
Expanding into hydrogen-based energy systems
DheyaTech is also working on fuel-flexible and hydrogen-based propulsion and power generation technologies.
Its DET 60 hydrogen flex-fuel micro turbogenerator has a maximum power output of 60 kW, according to the startup's product specifications.
DheyaTech has also developed a hydrogen anode blower for fuel-cell applications. A high-speed induction motor integrated with the blower has received EU ATEX certification for use in Zone 2 hazardous environments.
The startup has also developed a hydrogen-based flexi-fuel combustor in collaboration with the Indian Institute of Science in Bengaluru for its 60 kW flexi-fuel turbogenerator.
Vikas Verma, Partner at Avaana Capital, said, “The next generation of Indian deep tech companies will not just adapt technologies developed elsewhere; they will build globally relevant platforms from the ground up. DheyaTech represents that shift - building differentiated, mission-critical technology in a sector of strategic importance to India. We believe the company has the potential to become a global leader in propulsion, and we are excited to partner with the team as they take Indian engineering to markets around the world.”
DheyaTech's funding comes as other Indian companies step up work on gas turbine and propulsion technologies for aerospace and power applications.
For DheyaTech, the latest funding marks a move from technology development towards wider production, testing and commercial deployment as it seeks customers in India and overseas.
