india-882a33c5de.headline: In India’s capital, Delhiites reduced to documents
india-882a33c5de.source: India Latest News: Top National Headlines Today & Breaking News | The Hindu
india-882a33c5de.fulltext:
Aadhaar number. PAN card. Voter ID. Ration card. Sanichari Devi, 63, has packed all of these documents into a polythene bag for the special intensive revision (SIR) hearing at the Government Sarvodaya Bal Vidyalaya, a government school near Mori Gate in Delhi’s Chandni Chowk Assembly constituency on September 15.
These were the papers by which the State had recognised her, again and again, as a citizen all these years, she claims. But that afternoon they were not enough.
“First, the official at the hearing asked me to bring a bank passbook for which I had to return home,” she says. Home is about two kilometres away in an overcrowded Chandni Chowk locality. “When I came back panting, I was again sent another kilometre to get a photocopy of the documents,” she says on this errand alone.
“Tum log hai na padha likha toh bhi nahi bujha raha hai ki ka ka chahiye, hum toh hain hi angootha chaap, [You are all educated; even then you’re not telling us clearly what documents are needed. I am unlettered],” she says, distressed by the officials’ impatience and their cryptic responses.
For nearly two hours, Devi, who claims her name was on the 2002 electoral roll in Bihar, where she was born, clutches her papers trying to understand the process of staying on India’s electoral roll. She is surrounded by 70 to 80 people, all with similar problems.
Devi is a daily-wage earner. Her ₹400-500 for the day is lost, and she has no idea how to pay for her family of three, including two grandsons. Her son and daughter-in-law are no more. Exhausted from walking and distressed from losing a day’s wage, Devi faints in the afternoon sun. Two men catch her before she falls and help her to a chair.
The government school in Chandni Chowk is one of the three locations in this Assembly constituency where SIR hearings are taking place. These hearings are for voters who had notices served to them for anomalies, like name mismatches, and for being unmapped — meaning their names or relatives’ names were not found on older SIR rolls.
At every hearing location, 100 to 1,000 people turn up every day with documents to prove that they are eligible to vote. Once they are there, many find that none of their documents match the 11 ID proofs prescribed by the Election Commission of India for the SIR. The exercise, rolled out in 2025 just before the Bihar Assembly election, was intended to clean up voter lists by identifying duplicate entries and removing the names of those who have died, moved from their addresses, or are illegal migrants. But since it was rolled out, and now having covered 30 of India’s States and Union Territories, over 13 crore people on the voter list have been removed during the draft stage. This has become the subject of intense public debate, with concerns that genuine voters are being left out, particularly those who struggle to navigate a documentation-heavy process.
The scale of deletions has been striking in Delhi. Of 1.45 crore people who were on the rolls on June 16, 2026, only 97.5 lakh remain. Around 47.6 lakh people have been marked Absent, Shifted, Dead and Duplicate (ASDD) as reasons for their exclusion at the draft stage. Of the 97.5 lakh on the list, more than one-third on the draft rolls face notices. These will be disposed of by October 29 after they submit their documents either online or at the hearing centres. The final roll will be published on November 4.
Physical and mental stress
At an SIR hearing centre in Rajouri Garden’s government boys’ school, the queue snakes past five rows of Booth Level Officers (BLOs) and Assistant Electoral Registration Officers (AEROs) seated at desks with laptops. Each family in the line carries a folder of documents collected over decades. Every day, around 500 cases are scheduled for hearing here.
Ram Chandar, 55, from Etah in Uttar Pradesh, has lived in Delhi for 37 years, working at a housekeeping service. He says he has voted during the tenures of Sheila Dikshit and Arvind Kejriwal, and in the last election when Rekha Gupta came to power. But this time, all his family members, including his parents, wife, brother, and sister-in-law, received notices stating that they had failed to provide details of themselves or a relative from the 2002 SIR rolls.
He is among more than 13.79 lakh people who have been served notices in Delhi after being marked “unmapped”; another 19.33 lakh were flagged for “logical discrepancies”, including name mismatches and age-related anomalies. Even after submitting his previous voter ID, his identification could not be established.
“They want illiterate people like us to provide such minute details that date back to 2002, while officials themselves are so careless that they sent me a notice for September 14, even though there was a UPSC and NDA entrance exam at this centre. If they cannot keep an account of a month’s calendar, how are we supposed to keep everything in place for years?” he says. His mother and sister-in-law, he says, would not be able to attend the hearing as they were in the village for a family function. “Will their names be deleted forever?” he wonders.
After a three-hour wait, when he climbs onto the stage where officials sit, the BLO takes barely a minute to answer his queries and sends him back with a list of additional documents to bring.
A few places behind him, Seema (name changed to protect privacy), 31, is helping her husband Rahul (name changed to protect privacy) navigate the same scrutiny. “Waise to tum logon ko unke kapdon se pehchaan lete hain; ab humein nahi pehchaan rahe ki hum tumhare desh ke hain ki nahi? [You can recognise people by their clothes, but now you can’t even recognise whether we belong to your country or not?]” she asks.
In 2019, Prime Minister Narendra Modi had said at a rally in Jharkhand (amid protests against the Citizenship Amendment Act, which was passed that year) that people could identify “aag lagane wale [arsonists]” by their clothes. In Rahul’s case, the only discrepancy was that his father’s name Mahavir was spelled “Mahaveer” on his voter ID. “They asked me to get this corrected and appeal for another hearing,” he says. If Ram Chandar and Rahul were undone by mismatched records, others were undone by the process itself.
Preeti Bora Mondal, 44, received a physical notice for a hearing on September 12, but missed it because of an official event scheduled a month earlier. “Now I got a notice over the phone for October 7. The notice reads that if I have any query, I can contact my BLO. But when I did, she never picked up,” she says. She adds, “They are serving us these notices as if we are criminals or have done something wrong.”
Most recipients didn’t know they could submit their documents online. The website link is available via a QR code on the notice.
Paramjeet Thukral, 55, who has recently moved to her parents’ home in Tagore Garden from south Delhi, says she did try to do everything online, but was unsuccessful as the system said she didn’t have the right documents. “I had attached everything which was needed,” she says, adding that if even half the time the government was spending on the exercise had gone into the city instead, “the roads would be better and the city cleaner.”
Manoj (name changed to protect privacy) and his family of five, who were also at the centre to respond to a notice, had received assurance that their enrolments would stand. His 80-year-old grandmother didn’t get this assurance, despite having voted in at least 10 State and Central elections. “So many illegal votes are cast in every election; they are not vigilant at that time,” he says. Seema, still nearby, is less measured: “Agli baar aane do inko vote maangne, tab bataayenge [The next time let them come asking for our votes; then we’ll teach them a lesson].” She is furious at the two-day wage loss her husband has suffered to get their names enrolled in the voter list and is worried about the cost of the Internet café and corrections still ahead of them.
“They want illiterate people like us to provide such minute details that date back to 2002, while officials themselves are so careless that they sent me a notice for September 14, despite the fact that there was a UPSC and NDA entrance exam at this centre. If they cannot keep an account of a month’s calendar, how are we supposed to keep everything in place for years?”Ram ChandarHousekeeping worker
The confusion around documents
The AERO, Prabhas Kumar, who is attending to queries alone at Devi’s centre, says 7,000 notices had been generated at the centre comprising 50 booths of Chandni Chowk and BLOs are on the field to serve these notices to the people.
On the day Devi visited his station, he said that none of the people had the required documents. “But we are not turning them away. We are taking whatever they are bringing, from a Class 5 marksheet to a discharge card from the hospital where they were born,” Prabhas said, adding that even after maximum consideration, at least 50 people are turned away every day because they do not have a single valid document.
As per the ECI’s Standard Operating Procedure for the SIR, submitting only Aadhaar as a document is not sufficient.
Even though the 11 documents included educational certificates, this did not solve the problem for Yashoda Devi, 36. She sat restlessly outside the hall after being told that her Class 12 certificate, which she had spent a day looking for, would not be accepted because it did not mention her date of birth.
“I only have this. I don’t have a passport or a house in my name. My Class 10 certificate was destroyed when my parents’ house in Varanasi caught fire,” she says. Prabhas says a bank passbook could be attached as proof of date of birth, but he is unsure if it will be accepted.
In Rajouri Garden, several people say they are being asked to provide PAN cards. “I had my Class 10 CBSE marksheet and passport for age proof, yet the BLO kept insisting on a PAN card. When I resisted, saying it was not in the list of 11 documents shared with us, he took the marksheet,” says an attendee at the centre who did not wish to be named.
Electoral Registration Officer (ERO) Iti Agarwal, however, refuted the claim that PAN was being forced on people. “We are taking the PAN card as an additional document for proof of date of birth in cases where the elector has brought no document from those listed by the EC, or where the document provided is unsatisfactory. It is not mandatory since it is not a listed document,” she says. Even though hearings are scheduled in three time slots from the morning to 5 p.m., people in early slots end up waiting until the evening due to the lack of documents, and some return without a chance of hearing in a given slot. Their hearings are rescheduled.
Ader Khan, 52, has come directly from his daily-wage job in Wazirpur after taking half a day off with his wife, Heena Khan, for their 3-5 p.m. slot. However, when they asked for a token, they were turned away and told to come the next day or wait until 7.30 p.m.
“On one day, there are 300 people scheduled to attend a hearing. Not all show up. Of those who do, the desk can process only 120-130 cases due to a paucity of time,” says Kumar. As people surround the desk with their doubts, Kumar yells at a BLO who isn’t working at the centre but came for her own hearing. “You yourself don’t know what you have to do. It is because of this that so many people have been served notices. If BLOs had done their job properly, then all these people wouldn’t be standing here with their notices today.”
A BLO from North-east Delhi says the training was minimal and women, who have been appointed as teachers and now must do this work, are expected to go door to door. “How do you expect a woman to knock on a door when the smell of liquor reaches you even before the door is opened?” she says.

india-2ab7f822b6.headline: Govt says, there will be no charges at all for person-to-person UPI transactions, irrespective of amount transferred
india-2ab7f822b6.fulltext:
Government has clarified that there will be no charges at all for person-to-person (P2P) UPI transactions, irrespective of the amount transferred.
Finance Ministry said that payments to merchants up to two thousand rupees, along with transactions covered under the zero Merchant Discount Rate (MDR) framework for small merchants, will also remain free.
The Ministry said that consequently, approximately 96 percent of all P2M transactions will remain unaffected. It said that MDR will apply only to specified merchant transactions above two thousand rupees.
The Ministry said that MDR is neither a tax nor a charge collected by the government or the National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI). It is distributed among payment ecosystem participants, including banks and payment application providers, to support the operation and continued expansion of the UPI ecosystem.
NPCI has said that a revised UPI Merchant Discount Rate framework has been introduced on select merchant transactions, effective from 15th of next month, while keeping UPI free for consumers.
Akashavni correspondent reports said that a dedicated fund for promoting use of UPI by small merchants will be set up with a contribution of 5 percent of total MDR collections.
The Finance Ministry said that charges will apply only to person-to-merchant (P2M) transactions exceeding two thousand rupees. It said that UPI app providers are explicitly prohibited from levying platform fees or hidden charges.
The Ministry said that banks have been advised to ensure that merchants do not pass Merchant Discount Rate (MDR) charges to customers for UPI payments.
A nominal MDR of 0.4 percent will be levied on person-to-merchant transactions above 2,000 rupees, while for high-value transactions of 75 thousand rupees and above, MDR will be capped at three hundred rupees per transaction.
The Ministry informed that small merchants receiving up to one lakh rupees per month via UPI QR codes under the Person to Person Merchant (P2PM) classification will continue to enjoy mandatory zero MDR for all transactions.
Additionally, Railways, telecom, insurance, fuel sectors, agriculture inputs will pay a flat MDR of five rupees per transaction above two thousand rupees. It said there are no monthly quotas, volume limits, or tiered caps on free UPI transactions for individuals.
The Ministry said that the MDR framework has been introduced under the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007, following detailed deliberations by the UPI Steering Committee on the applicable rates, operational arrangements and consumer safeguards.
The framework seeks to strengthen the long-term sustainability of UPI while keeping payments free for individuals and protecting small merchants.

india-4afaf656bb.headline: India Mandates Aadhaar Biometric Checks for Subsidised LPG Refills
india-4afaf656bb.fulltext:
India Mandates Aadhaar Biometric Checks for Subsidised LPG Refills
India’s Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas has announced that domestic LPG consumers must complete biometric Aadhaar authentication to continue booking subsidised refill cylinders at regulated retail prices from 1 October 2026. According to the official government release, 27.43 crore active consumers, representing 89.9% of users, have already completed the process. The policy is intended to improve subsidy targeting, reduce duplicate or ineligible connections and limit the diversion of subsidised cylinders for commercial or industrial use.
The move forms part of India’s broader digital governance agenda, which increasingly relies on authenticated digital identity systems to improve service delivery. Recent initiatives linked to Aadhaar-based digital identity tools and wider discussions on digital governance frameworks have highlighted the government’s focus on improving transparency and reducing leakages in welfare programmes.
Authentication Required for Subsidised LPG Refills
From 1 October 2026, consumers who have not completed biometric Aadhaar authentication will need to do so before they can book LPG refills at subsidised regulated retail prices. Consumers who have already completed authentication will not be required to repeat the process and will continue receiving refills as normal.
The ministry stated that the authentication process is designed to ensure that subsidised LPG reaches eligible households. By linking each LPG connection to an Aadhaar-verified consumer, authorities aim to remove duplicate accounts and strengthen accountability in subsidy delivery.
Multiple Channels Available for Verification
Consumers can complete biometric authentication through several channels. Verification can be carried out during LPG delivery using mobile applications operated by oil marketing companies, at distributor outlets or through official mobile applications used by LPG customers.
The ministry said self-service electronic Know Your Customer procedures are also available through mobile applications for Indane, Bharat Gas and HP Gas customers. Video tutorials explaining the process have been published on the PMUY portal.
Alternative Supply Option Without Subsidy
Consumers who are unwilling or unable to complete biometric authentication will still be able to access LPG supplies. However, they must register this preference through their oil marketing company’s digital channels, including web portals, mobile applications, WhatsApp chatbots, IVRS systems or other available platforms.
These consumers will receive LPG in 5 kg or 10 kg cylinders at prevailing market rates without subsidy support, subject to local availability.
Nationwide Outreach Campaign Expanded
The ministry said oil marketing companies have been conducting nationwide outreach activities since October 2023 to encourage consumers to complete authentication. More than 12 crore SMS and WhatsApp messages have been sent to users, while distributors and delivery personnel have contacted households directly.
Special enrolment camps have also been organised at distributor outlets, public locations and rural areas. Additional communication measures have included IVRS prompts during refill bookings, mobile notifications, newspaper advertisements and social media campaigns.
The deadline for completing authentication was initially set for 30 June 2026 but was subsequently extended several times, including extensions to 31 July, 7 August, 15 August, 23 August, 31 August, 7 September and finally 14 September 2026.
Government Seeks to Contain Subsidy Costs
The ministry noted that domestic LPG continues to be sold below cost. In September 2026, the implicit subsidy on a standard 14.2 kg cylinder was around ₹210 (approximately US$2.50). In June 2026, the subsidy level had reached ₹721 (approximately US$8.60) per cylinder.
To maintain affordability, the government provided compensation of ₹22,000 crore (approximately US$2.6 billion) to oil marketing companies during the 2022-23 financial year. It is also providing ₹30,000 crore (approximately US$3.6 billion) during both the 2025-26 and 2026-27 financial years.
Despite these measures, the ministry said the cumulative gap between the cost and sale price of domestic LPG borne by public sector oil marketing companies had exceeded ₹62,000 crore (approximately US$7.4 billion) as of 31 August 2026.
The government has urged consumers who have not yet completed biometric Aadhaar authentication to do so before 1 October 2026. Assistance related to LPG services remains available through the toll-free helpline.

other-interests-1882f85dcd.fulltext:
In the first-known naval engagement between uncrewed vessels, a Ukrainian robot boat sank a Russian opponent in the Black Sea.
The action between the remote-controlled uncrewed surface vessels (USVs), or sea drones, took place earlier this month. A video released by the Ukrainian Navy shows its USV, identified as a Sargan-3000, firing a 12.7-millimetre heavy machine gun at the Russian vessel, which appears to be of the Orcan type, until it sinks.
Both sea drones are propelled by water jets. The Sargan is around 7 metres long with a top speed of over 80 kilometres per hour, while the Orcan is about 5 metres long and can reach 64 km/h.
Advertisement
This is the first-known clash of its type in the history of naval warfare, according to independent naval expert H. I. Sutton. But it didn’t come as a surprise.
“It was inevitable that there would be USV-on-USV combat,” says Sutton. “We have seen the same in the air, and on the ground.”
Ukraine developed USVs after scuttling its only major warship early in 2022 to prevent its capture. In October 2022, Ukraine carried out a successful attack with seven sea drones, damaging a Russian frigate and a minesweeper at the Sevastopol naval base in Crimea.
Since then, Ukraine has moved from improvised USVs based on speedboats and jet-powered watercraft to advanced designs, including the Magura and Sea Baby series. In conjunction with shore-based anti-ship missiles and aerial drones, Ukraine’s uncrewed vessels have sunk or damaged a third of the Russian Black Sea fleet. The remainder is now largely confined to port behind booms and other defences.
Initially, Ukraine’s USVs carried explosive charges for one-way attacks. More advanced versions are now armed with surface-to-air missiles, with one Ukrainian USV being the first ever to shoot down a helicopter, in 2024. Others are fitted with machine guns and unguided rockets. Some Ukrainian USVs are miniature aircraft carriers, launching aerial drones.
From 2024, the Russians copied Ukraine, building small, fast USVs with explosive warheads to attack ports, bridges and shipping. The Russian Orcan in this month’s action was likely to have been heading towards the Ukrainian port city of Odesa as part of a campaign targeting cargo ships.
“It was a small vessel with an explosive charge and no gun turret, intended for an offensive operation ramming a larger vessel,” says Sutton. “The Ukrainian one was armed with a machine gun, showing that it had a more defensive role. So, it was to be expected, although not guaranteed, that the Ukrainian one would win this duel.”
Sutton says the action is likely to drive further evolution of USVs on both sides. Just as helicopters being used against sea drones led to the design of new models equipped with surface-to-air missiles, attack USVs may start carrying machine guns or other defensive weaponry, or travel with escorts.
This first robot naval action is unlikely to be the last. “Probably in future we will see Ukrainian USVs interdicted by Russian ones close to Russian naval bases,” says Sutton.
Naval experts believe the Black Sea campaign is a special case, saying that its lessons may not apply in other theatres of operation where actions take place over much greater ranges and timescales. But the continued rise of robot boats is another sign of warfare’s changing face.

India Art Fair’s EDI+IONS brings 18 galleries to Ahmedabad
Gallery walkthroughs, exhibitions, artist open studios, music and conversations are being held across the city
Ahmedabad’s art scene has found a new platform as India Art Fair’s travelling EDI+IONS opened at Baronet House in Shahibaug this week, bringing together 18 galleries, design participants and an institution from across India.
The second edition of EDI+IONS, which follows its launch in Hyderabad last year, includes five Ahmedabad galleries — 079 | Stories Art Gallery, Archer Art Gallery, Iram Modern, Samara Art Gallery and ZOCA — alongside galleries from Mumbai, Delhi, Kolkata and Chennai.
Jaya Asokan, fair director, India Art Fair said that Ahmedabad had long held an important place in India’s cultural landscape, shaped by generations of artists, architects, designers, craftspeople, collectors and patrons.
“With this edition, we want to celebrate that legacy while creating new connections between the city’s creative community and voices from across the country. At its heart, EDI+IONS is about bringing people together around art and culture, strengthening regional ecosystems and creating meaningful opportunities for exchange beyond our annual fair in Delhi,” she said.
Meha Patel, vice chairperson, Zydus Foundation, which has supported the Ahmedabad edition, said the city needed a platform that could take its existing creative depth to a wider audience.
“With its rich textile history, design pedigree and architectural ambition, Ahmedabad does not need an introduction to the art world; it needs a platform that allows its existing depth to speak to a wider audience,” she said.
Patel said the initiative could create greater visibility and market access for local and aspiring artists, artisans and craftspeople.
The fair is being held at the century-old Indo-Gothic Baronet House and extends beyond the venue. Gallery walkthroughs, exhibitions, artist open studios, music and conversations are being held across the city.
Among the exhibitions is Truth is Stranger Than Fiction, a ceramic sculptural series by Khanjan Dalal, while Archer Art Gallery is presenting Parikrama, a solo presentation by Ganesh Gohain. A GALLERYSKE-MCAA collaboration will present I Dwell in Possibility at the Museum of Contemporary Art Ahmedabad’s Satellite Venue.
The wider programme also extends to venues across the city, including the Calico Museum of Textiles, Shreyas Folk Museum, House of MG, Kanoria Centre for Arts and Amdavad ni Gufa.
Hardeep Singh Brar, president and chief executive officer,, BMW Group India, said the company was pleased to continue its partnership with India Art Fair as the presenting partner of IAF EDI+IONS Ahmedabad.
“As this travelling format expands to new cities, it reflects our shared commitment to fostering meaningful cultural exchange and creating new opportunities for audiences to engage with modern and contemporary art and design. Ahmedabad, with its rich artistic and architectural heritage, spirit of craftsmanship, and culture of innovation, provides a compelling setting for this next chapter,” he said.

Call For Applications: Climate Intervention Environmental Impact Fund 2026 Up to $75,000 Grant
The Climate Intervention Environmental Impact Fund (CIEIF) is inviting applications from investigators and organisations developing innovative climate-intervention technologies that are approaching small-scale field testing.
The fund will award three grants of $75,000 each in its sixth grant round. Funding will support environmental impact assessments, predictive impact modelling and stakeholder engagement linked to proposed climate-intervention field tests.
The application deadline is December 1, 2026.
What Is the CIEIF Grant?
The Climate Intervention Environmental Impact Fund supports projects that aim to address the root causes of global warming or its major effects through innovative climate-intervention technologies.
Rather than funding the development or general implementation of a climate project, CIEIF provides grants for the analysis and stakeholder engagement needed to assess the potential environmental, social, economic and health impacts of a proposed field test.
The current funding round will make three awards of $75,000 each.
What Can the $75,000 Grant Fund?
Applicants must show how the funding will be used primarily for at least one of three areas:
- Environmental impact assessment (EIA)
- Predictive environmental impact modelling
- Engagement with potentially affected stakeholders, including communities and government agencies
The grant can cover relevant consultant costs, applicant staff time and closely associated expenses connected to this work.
Selected applicants will receive the first third of the grant after discussions with CIEIF about the expert consulting needs of their proposed field test. The remaining payments will follow an agreed schedule linked to project milestones.
Who Can Apply?
CIEIF accepts applications from qualified investigators and organisations developing innovative climate-intervention technologies that are approaching field testing.
The fund has a global reach and can consider applications from private businesses. However, it gives higher priority to nonprofit institutions, including academic institutions. International projects may receive higher priority where a US nonprofit partner is available to accept the grant as a donation.
Individuals and student projects are not eligible.
What Types of Climate Projects Are Eligible?
CIEIF considers innovative interventions that could potentially be scaled to deliver meaningful climate benefits.
Examples listed by the fund include:
- Biochar
- Enhanced weathering
- Carbon dioxide removal methods other than Direct Air Capture
- Cloud brightening
- Ocean interventions and marine carbon removal
- Methane removal
- Livestock methane capture
- Agricultural climate interventions
- Ice and land albedo enhancement
- Greenhouse-gas-removing coatings
- Black soot removal or mitigation
- Nitrous oxide and chlorofluorocarbon removal
- Other similar climate-intervention technologies
The proposed intervention must be approaching a small-scale field test, rather than remaining at the basic research stage.
What Projects Are Not Eligible?
CIEIF does not provide general implementation or basic research funding.
Projects focused primarily on areas such as:
- Climate adaptation
- Clean energy
- Climate resilience
- General emissions reduction
- Sustainable development
are outside the fund’s scope unless the project involves an eligible climate intervention that addresses a root cause of global warming or its major effects.
The fund also excludes stratospheric or higher solar radiation management, as well as Carbon Capture Utilization and Storage (CCUS) and Direct Air Capture (DAC).
What Must Be Included in the Application?
There is no standard application form or template.
Applicants should prepare a grant request of no more than 20 single-spaced pages, using 12-point font and written in English. Biosketches and important scientific publications can be attached as supplementary material.
The application should address:
- Contact details and biosketches of the project personnel.
- A detailed description of the proposed field test and evidence that the technology is ready for testing.
- Expected technical and environmental challenges.
- Potential economic, social, public health and safety impacts.
- Required government permits and approvals.
- Previous publications relating to the technology.
- At least two independent consulting firms that could support the impact assessment, modelling or stakeholder-related work.
- A proposed budget showing how the $75,000 would be used.
- Other sources of funding for the investigation.
- Relevant insurance arrangements.
- Confirmation that the project’s results can be published.
- Any other important information about the proposed field test.
Important Application Requirement
CIEIF has specifically stated that AI-generated content cannot be used in cover letters or applications.
The organisation says applications will be reviewed for AI use and that applications identified as using AI-generated information will be rejected, with applicants potentially barred from future applications.
For this reason, applicants should prepare their submissions themselves and follow CIEIF’s instructions carefully.
How to Apply
There is no standard online application form.
Once the grant request is ready, applicants should contact Peter T. Jenkins, Manager, CIEIF, at [email protected]. CIEIF will then discuss the appropriate way to submit the application.
The fund says applications will be kept confidential.
For More Information, Visit the Official website: Climate Intervention Environmental Impact Fund
Deadline
The deadline for the sixth CIEIF grant round is:
December 1, 2026
Grant decisions are expected to be announced by February 1, 2027.

Programme: Climate Intervention Environmental Impact Fund
Funding: $75,000 per selected project
Number of grants: 3
Focus: Environmental impact assessment, predictive impact modelling and stakeholder engagement
Geographic scope: Global
Eligible applicants: Qualified investigators and organisations
Priority: Nonprofit and academic institutions
Individuals: Not eligible
Application format: Grant request, maximum 20 pages
Deadline: December 1, 2026
Decision expected: February 1, 2027
Application: Contact CIEIF before submission

NUPRC Gives Oil Licence Holders October Deadline to Meet Work Commitments
The Nigerian Upstream Petroleum Regulatory Commission (NUPRC) has warned holders of non-performing oil licences that they risk losing their acreages if they fail to meet approved work commitments.
The regulator has given affected operators until October 31, 2026 to disclose their compliance status, explain challenges delaying operations and submit revised plans for meeting their obligations.
The directive covers Petroleum Prospecting Licences awarded under the 2020 Marginal Field Bid Round, 2022/2023 Mini Bid Round and 2024 Licensing Round.
The warning was contained in a circular dated September 14, 2026 and signed by NUPRC Chief Executive, Oritsemeyiwa Eyesan.
NUPRC Moves to Enforce Drill-or-Drop Rule
The commission said it is moving to enforce the “Drill-or-Drop” provisions of the Petroleum Industry Act 2021, which require licence holders to carry out approved exploration and development activities within the terms of their licences.
NUPRC said enforcement measures could include refusing licence extensions, requiring operators to relinquish acreages, calling in work performance securities and commencing revocation proceedings.
The commission said the principle underlying the PIA is that oil and gas acreage is expected to be worked, adding that acreage not worked within its term returns to the Federal Government.
However, NUPRC said its objective is to increase oil and gas production rather than simply take licences away from operators.
“The Commission’s objective is to increase production, not forfeiture,” it stated.
Operators Asked to Explain Delays
NUPRC acknowledged that some operators may be unable to meet their work commitments because of challenges including financing, rig availability, insecurity, host-community engagement, infrastructure, regulatory approvals and disagreements among partners.
Affected operators are required to provide details of their level of compliance with licence obligations, including progress on their approved work programmes.
They must also identify the specific challenges affecting their operations and submit proposed measures and revised timelines for addressing them by October 31.
The commission said it is prepared to facilitate the resolution of issues within its statutory mandate.
However, discussions with NUPRC will not extend the term of a licence or suspend an operator’s legal obligations.
The regulator also warned that disputes between partners would not excuse a failure to meet licence commitments.
At Least 62 Awardees Identified
The latest enforcement action affects licences issued through three recent licensing exercises.
at least 62 successful awardees have been identified across the 2020 Marginal Field Bid Round, 2022/2023 Mini Bid Round and 2024 Licensing Round. The October 31 deadline, however, applies specifically to licence holders whose acreages are not meeting their approved work commitments.
The 2020 Marginal Field Bid Round resulted in the award of 50 Petroleum Prospecting Licences, while licences were also awarded through the 2022/2023 Mini Bid Round and the 2024 Licensing Round.
NUPRC said the latest directive is intended to ensure that licensed acreages are actively explored and developed rather than held without corresponding work and investment.
The circular is a general advisory and does not itself constitute a formal notice of default under the Petroleum Industry Act or its subsidiary regulations.
